item.title: HTML Headings
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Headings are the titles and subtitles of a page. Readers scan them to decide what to read, screen readers use them to jump around, and search engines use them to understand what each part of the page is about. Getting headings right is one of the easiest ways to make a page better.

Six levels of headings

HTML has six heading elements, from <h1> (most important) to <h6> (least important):

<h1>Heading level 1</h1>
<h2>Heading level 2</h2>
<h3>Heading level 3</h3>
<h4>Heading level 4</h4>
<h5>Heading level 5</h5>
<h6>Heading level 6</h6>

Browsers show <h1> largest and boldest, and each level after it a little smaller. But the size is only the default look. What really matters is the level, because it describes how important the heading is and where it sits in the page's outline.

Headings build an outline

Think of a page like a book. The <h1> is the book title, each <h2> is a chapter, and each <h3> is a section inside a chapter.

<h1>Healthy Breakfast Ideas</h1>

<h2>Quick breakfasts</h2>
<h3>Overnight oats</h3>
<p>Mix oats with milk and leave them in the fridge.</p>
<h3>Banana toast</h3>
<p>Toast, peanut butter and a sliced banana.</p>

<h2>Weekend breakfasts</h2>
<h3>Vegetable omelette</h3>
<p>Eggs, onions, tomatoes and spinach.</p>

If you read only the headings, you understand the whole page: the topic, the two groups, and the dishes in each. That's the test of a good heading structure.

Rules for a clean outline

One h1 per page

The <h1> is the main title of the page. Use it once. On a blog, it is the post title; on a lesson page like this one, it is the lesson name.

Don't skip levels

Go from <h2> to <h3>, not from <h2> straight to <h5>. Skipping levels confuses screen reader users, who often navigate by heading level.

<!-- Avoid -->
<h2>Our services</h2>
<h5>Web design</h5>

<!-- Better -->
<h2>Our services</h2>
<h3>Web design</h3>

Going back up is fine: after an <h3> you can start a new <h2> section.

Choose headings by meaning, not by size

Never pick <h4> just because you like its smaller size. Pick the level that fits the outline, and change the size later with CSS. You'll learn how in the CSS lessons.

Headings and accessibility

Many blind and low-vision users browse with a screen reader. A common habit is to press a key that jumps from heading to heading, like skimming. A page with clear headings is quick to explore; a page with no headings is one long wall of text read aloud from top to bottom.

Headings and search engines

Google reads your headings to understand the topics on the page. A heading like <h2>How to boil eggs</h2> tells it far more than a bold paragraph that says the same thing. Write headings for people first: short, specific and descriptive. That's also what works best for search.

Don't use headings just to make text big or bold

<!-- Wrong: this isn't a title, just a sentence someone wanted to stand out -->
<h3>Free delivery on all orders today!</h3>

If the text isn't a title for the content that follows, use a paragraph and make it stand out with <strong> or CSS instead.

Common mistakes

  • Several h1 elements on one page for decoration. Keep one main title.
  • Skipping levels (h2 → h4) to get a smaller font.
  • Using headings for styling text that isn't a title.
  • Vague headings like "Section 2" or "More info". Say what the section contains.

Exercise

Open the breakfast example with Try it Yourself and:

  1. Add a third <h2> section called "Breakfasts for kids" with two <h3> dishes.
  2. Write one paragraph under each new dish.
  3. Read only the headings out loud. Does the outline make sense on its own?
  4. Change one <h3> into <h5> and notice how the outline now "jumps". Change it back.

Summary

  • HTML has six heading levels, <h1> to <h6>.
  • Headings form an outline: one <h1>, then <h2> sections, then <h3> sub-sections.
  • Don't skip levels and don't choose a level for its size.
  • Good headings help readers, screen reader users and search engines.

Next, you'll learn about paragraphs, line breaks and horizontal rules.
item.excerpt:encoded: The six heading levels from h1 to h6, how to build a clear outline with them, and why headings matter for readers, screen readers and Google.

item.title: HTML Paragraphs
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Most of the text on the web lives in paragraphs. In this lesson you'll learn how the <p> element works, how browsers treat spaces and line breaks in your code, and three related elements: <br>, <hr> and <pre>.

The p element

A paragraph starts with <p> and ends with </p>:

<p>This is the first paragraph. It can be as long as you like.</p>
<p>This is the second paragraph. Browsers add space above and below each one.</p>

Each paragraph is a block: it starts on a new line and takes the full width available. The browser adds a margin before and after it, so paragraphs are visually separated without any extra work.

Browsers collapse white space

This surprises almost every beginner. Extra spaces and line breaks in your HTML code are ignored. Any run of spaces, tabs and new lines is shown as a single space.

<p>
  This     paragraph
  has lots of      spaces
  and line breaks      in the code.
</p>

In the browser, this shows as one normal line of text: "This paragraph has lots of spaces and line breaks in the code."

This is actually useful: you can indent and wrap your code however you like to keep it readable, and the page still looks clean.

Line breaks with br

To break a line inside a paragraph without starting a new paragraph, use <br>:

<p>
  VitalStack<br>
  Learn to code, one lesson at a time<br>
  contact@example.com
</p>

<br> is an empty element: it has no closing tag. Use it where a line break is part of the content, such as addresses, poems or song lyrics.

Don't use several <br> tags to create space between blocks. That's a job for separate paragraphs or for CSS margins.

<!-- Avoid -->
<p>First idea.<br><br><br>Second idea.</p>

<!-- Better -->
<p>First idea.</p>
<p>Second idea.</p>

Horizontal rules with hr

<hr> marks a change of topic between paragraphs. Browsers draw it as a horizontal line.

<p>That's everything about the morning schedule.</p>
<hr>
<p>Now let's look at the afternoon.</p>

Like <br>, it has no closing tag. Use it for a thematic break, not as decoration. If you just want a line for looks, add a border with CSS later.

Preformatted text with pre

Sometimes spaces and line breaks do matter, for example in ASCII art, poems laid out in a special way, or plain-text output. The <pre> element keeps every space and line break exactly as you typed it, and shows the text in a monospace font.

<pre>
Name      Score
Asha        92
Rohan       87
Meera       95
</pre>

The columns line up because nothing is collapsed. <pre> is also commonly used together with <code> to show blocks of program code.

Choosing the right element

Common mistakes

  • Expecting Enter to make a new line. Pressing Enter in your code does nothing on the page. Use a new <p> or a <br>.
  • **Using <br><br> for spacing.** Make separate paragraphs instead.
  • **Putting a heading or list inside <p>.** A paragraph can only contain text and inline elements. The browser will close the paragraph early and your layout will break.
  • **Forgetting the closing </p>.** Browsers often guess correctly, but not always. Close every paragraph.

Exercise

  1. Write three short paragraphs about your favourite food.
  2. Add your (made-up) postal address using one paragraph and <br> tags.
  3. Separate two topics with an <hr>.
  4. Make a small table of three friends and their ages using <pre>, and line up the columns with spaces.

Summary

  • <p> creates a paragraph; browsers add space around it.
  • Extra spaces and new lines in your code collapse into one space.
  • <br> breaks a line inside a block; <hr> marks a change of topic.
  • <pre> keeps spacing exactly as written, in a monospace font.

Next, you'll learn how to make text bold, italic, highlighted and more with text formatting elements.
item.excerpt:encoded: How the p element works, why browsers ignore your extra spaces, and when to use line breaks, horizontal rules and pre for preformatted text.

item.title: HTML Text Formatting
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
HTML has a set of small elements that change how a few words look or what they mean: important words, emphasis, highlighted text, chemical formulas and more. These are inline elements: they sit inside a line of text instead of starting a new block.

Strong and em: meaning

<p><strong>Warning:</strong> turn off the power before opening the case.</p>
<p>I <em>really</em> want to learn JavaScript this month.</p>
  • <strong> marks text as important. Browsers show it in bold.
  • <em> marks emphasis, the stress you'd put on a word when speaking. Browsers show it in italics.

Screen readers can change their voice for these elements, and search engines understand that the words matter. Emphasis changes meaning, too: "I *really* want" is different from "*I* really want".

B and i: style without extra importance

<p>The <b>Pro</b> plan includes everything in Basic.</p>
<p>The word <i lang="fr">bonjour</i> means hello.</p>
  • <b> makes text bold without saying it is important, e.g. product names or key words in a summary.
  • <i> sets text apart without emphasis: foreign words, technical terms, names of ships or books, thoughts.

Rule of thumb: if you'd stress it when reading aloud, use <em>; if it's important, use <strong>. If it only needs to look different, use <b> or <i>.

Highlighted, small, deleted and inserted text

<p>Search results for <mark>flexbox</mark> in this lesson.</p>
<p><small>Prices include tax.</small></p>
<p>Price: <del>₹999</del> <ins>₹499</ins></p>
  • <mark> highlights text that is relevant right now, like search matches. It gets a yellow background by default.
  • <small> is for side comments and fine print: copyright notes, legal text.
  • <del> shows text that was removed (drawn with a line through it).
  • <ins> shows text that was added (underlined).

<del> and <ins> are perfect for showing price drops or edits to a document.

Subscript and superscript

<p>Water is H<sub>2</sub>O.</p>
<p>E = mc<sup>2</sup></p>
<p>Today is the 1<sup>st</sup> of the month.</p>
  • <sub> lowers the text: chemical formulas, maths indices.
  • <sup> raises the text: powers, footnote numbers, ordinals like 1st.

Code, keyboard keys and abbreviations

These are very useful on a programming site:

<p>Use the <code>console.log()</code> function to print a value.</p>
<p>Press <kbd>Ctrl</kbd> + <kbd>S</kbd> to save.</p>
<p><abbr title="HyperText Markup Language">HTML</abbr> is easy to learn.</p>
  • <code> marks a piece of computer code (shown in a monospace font).
  • <kbd> marks keys the user should press.
  • <abbr> marks an abbreviation; the title shows the full form when you hover over it.

Quotations

<p>As the saying goes, <q>practice makes perfect</q>.</p>

<blockquote cite="https://www.w3.org/">
  <p>The Web is for everyone.</p>
</blockquote>
  • <q> is a short quote inside a sentence; the browser adds the quotation marks.
  • <blockquote> is a longer quote shown as its own indented block. The cite attribute can point to the source.

Nesting formatting elements

You can combine them, as long as you close them in the reverse order:

<p><strong>Note: <em>do not</em> skip this step.</strong></p>

Common mistakes

  • **Using <b> for important warnings.** Use <strong> so the importance is in the code, not just the look.
  • Underlining normal text. Readers expect underlined text to be a link. Avoid <u> except for special cases like marking spelling errors.
  • Overusing bold. If everything is bold, nothing stands out. Pick a few words.
  • Wrong nesting like <strong><em>text</strong></em>. Close the inner element first.

Exercise

Write a short "product card" using only paragraphs and formatting:

  1. Product name in <b>, old price in <del> and new price in <ins>.
  2. One important note with <strong> and one emphasised word with <em>.
  3. A fine-print line with <small>.
  4. A tip that says to press Ctrl + P to print, using <kbd>.
  5. Bonus: write the formula for carbon dioxide (CO2) with <sub>.

Summary

  • <strong> = important, <em> = emphasis; <b> and <i> only change the look.
  • <mark>, <small>, <del>, <ins>, <sub> and <sup> cover most other formatting needs.
  • <code>, <kbd> and <abbr> are handy for technical writing.
  • Use <q> and <blockquote> for quotations.

Next, you'll learn the most important element of the web: links.
item.excerpt:encoded: Bold, italic, highlighted, small, deleted, inserted, subscript and superscript text, and the difference between strong and b, em and i.

item.title: HTML Links
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Links are what make the web a *web*. With one element, <a>, you can connect a page to any other page in the world, to a section of the same page, to an email address or to a phone number.

The a element

<a href="https://developer.mozilla.org/">MDN Web Docs</a>
  • <a> stands for anchor.
  • href (hypertext reference) is the address the link goes to.
  • The text between the tags is what the reader sees and clicks.

By default, browsers show unvisited links blue and underlined, and visited links purple. You'll restyle them with CSS later.

Absolute and relative URLs

An absolute URL contains the full address, including https:// and the domain. Use it to link to other websites:

<a href="https://www.python.org/">Python's official site</a>

A relative URL is a path from the current page. Use it for pages on your own site:

<a href="about.html">About (same folder)</a>
<a href="blog/first-post.html">First post (inside the blog folder)</a>
<a href="../index.html">Home (one folder up)</a>
<a href="/contact/">Contact (from the site root)</a>
  • No slash at the start: relative to the current folder.
  • ../ goes up one folder.
  • A slash at the start (/contact/) starts from the root of the website.

Relative links keep working if you move the whole site to another domain, which is why sites use them internally.

Opening a link in a new tab

<a href="https://github.com/" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">GitHub</a>

target="_blank" opens the link in a new tab. Add rel="noopener noreferrer" so the new page can't control your page through JavaScript (modern browsers do this automatically, but it's still a good habit).

Use new tabs sparingly. Readers can open a new tab themselves; forcing it can be confusing, especially on phones. A good rule: open in a new tab only when leaving the page would lose the reader's work, e.g. a link inside a half-filled form.

Linking to a section of a page

Give an element an id, then link to it with #:

<a href="#faq">Jump to the FAQ</a>

<!-- ... lots of content ... -->

<h2 id="faq">Frequently asked questions</h2>

Clicking the link scrolls straight to the heading. You can also combine it with a page address: href="guide.html#faq". The "On this page" box on VitalStack lessons works exactly like this.

Email and phone links

<a href="mailto:contact@example.com">Email us</a>
<a href="tel:+911234567890">Call us</a>

mailto: opens the reader's email app with the address filled in. tel: starts a call on phones. Note that email addresses in page code can be collected by spam bots, so many sites use a contact form instead.

Download links

<a href="files/cheatsheet.pdf" download>Download the cheat sheet</a>

The download attribute asks the browser to save the file instead of opening it.

Write link text that makes sense on its own

Screen reader users often list all the links on a page, and search engines use link text to understand the target page. "Click here" tells them nothing.

<!-- Avoid -->
<p>To learn about images, <a href="html-images.html">click here</a>.</p>

<!-- Better -->
<p>Next, learn how to <a href="html-images.html">add images to a page</a>.</p>

The title attribute

<a href="html-forms.html" title="Lesson 15: HTML Forms">Forms</a>

title shows a small tooltip on hover. It's a nice extra, but don't put important information only there: phone users and many screen reader users never see it.

Common mistakes

  • **Missing https://** in external links: href="google.com" is treated as a file in your own folder.
  • "Click here" link text. Describe the destination instead.
  • Spaces in file names like my page.html. Use hyphens: my-page.html.
  • **Linking to an id that doesn't exist** or has different spelling. #FAQ and #faq are different.

Exercise

  1. Make a link to your favourite website that opens in the same tab.
  2. Make a second link that opens in a new tab with the safe rel value.
  3. Add three <h2> sections with ids, and a small "table of contents" at the top with links to each.
  4. Add an email link that says "Write to me".

Summary

  • <a href="...">text</a> creates a link.
  • Use absolute URLs for other sites and relative URLs inside your own site.
  • #id links jump to a section; mailto: and tel: start emails and calls.
  • Write link text that describes where the link goes.

Next, you'll add pictures to your pages with images.
item.excerpt:encoded: Create links with the a element: absolute and relative URLs, opening links in a new tab safely, linking to a section, email and phone links, and writing good link text.

item.title: HTML Images
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Images make pages friendlier and easier to understand. In this lesson you'll add images with <img>, describe them for people who can't see them, and learn the habits that keep pages fast.

The img element

<img src="https://picsum.photos/id/1025/400/300" alt="A small dog wrapped in a blanket" width="400" height="300">
  • src (source) is the address of the image file, absolute or relative, just like a link.
  • alt (alternative text) describes the image.
  • width and height give the image's size in pixels.

<img> is an empty element: no closing tag.

Alt text: the most important attribute

Alt text is read aloud by screen readers, shown if the image fails to load, and used by search engines to understand the picture. Write what a person would need to know if they couldn't see it.

<!-- Too vague -->
<img src="chart.png" alt="chart">

<!-- Useful -->
<img src="chart.png" alt="Bar chart: Python is the most used language in the survey at 49%, JavaScript second at 41%">

Tips for good alt text:

  • Be specific and short; one sentence is usually enough.
  • Don't start with "Image of" or "Picture of". Screen readers already say it's an image.
  • If an image is pure decoration (a background swirl, a divider), use an empty alt: alt="". Screen readers then skip it. Never leave the attribute out completely.
  • If the image contains text, include that text in the alt.

Width and height prevent jumping pages

When a page loads, text often appears before images. If the browser doesn't know an image's size, it can't reserve space, so the text jumps down when the image arrives. Annoying for readers, and Google measures it as a quality signal ("layout shift").

Setting width and height to the image's real size lets the browser reserve the right space from the start. With CSS you can still make the image responsive later (max-width: 100%; height: auto;), and the browser keeps the correct proportions.

Image file formats

Large images are the most common reason pages load slowly. Resize a photo to the size it will actually be shown (there's no point sending a 4000-pixel photo for a 400-pixel box) and compress it.

Lazy loading

<img src="photo.jpg" alt="Sunset over the sea" width="800" height="533" loading="lazy">

loading="lazy" tells the browser to load the image only when the reader scrolls near it. Use it for images further down the page. Don't use it for the main image at the top; that one should load right away.

Images as links

Put an <img> inside an <a> to make it clickable:

<a href="https://www.w3.org/">
  <img src="https://picsum.photos/id/0/200/120" alt="Visit the W3C website" width="200" height="120">
</a>

When the image is the only content of a link, its alt text becomes the link text, so describe where the link goes.

Figures with captions

<figure>
  <img src="https://picsum.photos/id/1043/400/260" alt="A wooden desk with a laptop and a notebook" width="400" height="260">
  <figcaption>My study setup: one laptop, one notebook, no distractions.</figcaption>
</figure>

<figure> groups an image with its caption (<figcaption>). The caption is visible to everyone; the alt describes the image itself. They usually say different things.

Common mistakes

  • Missing alt attribute. Always include it, even if it's empty for decoration.
  • Wrong path. src="Images/Photo.JPG" and images/photo.jpg are different files on most servers. Paths are case-sensitive.
  • Huge files. Resize and compress before uploading.
  • Using images of text for headings or buttons. Real text is sharper, searchable and translatable.

Exercise

  1. Add an image from https://picsum.photos/id/237/300/200 with good alt text, and width and height.
  2. Wrap it in a <figure> with a caption.
  3. Make the image a link to any website.
  4. Add a second image further down with loading="lazy".

Summary

  • <img src="..." alt="..." width="..." height="..."> adds an image.
  • Alt text describes the image; use alt="" only for decoration.
  • Width and height stop the page from jumping while it loads.
  • Choose the right format, keep files small, and lazy-load images lower on the page.

Next, you'll organise content with ordered, unordered and description lists.
item.excerpt:encoded: Add images with the img element, write useful alt text, set width and height, choose the right file format and make images load fast with lazy loading.

item.title: HTML Lists
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Lists are everywhere: shopping lists, steps in a recipe, features of a product, the menu at the top of a website. HTML has three kinds of lists, and choosing the right one makes your content clearer for everyone.

Unordered lists

Use <ul> when the order doesn't matter. Each item goes in an <li> (list item):

<h3>Things to pack</h3>
<ul>
  <li>Laptop and charger</li>
  <li>Water bottle</li>
  <li>Notebook</li>
</ul>

Browsers show each item with a bullet point.

Ordered lists

Use <ol> when the order matters, such as steps or rankings:

<h3>Make a cup of tea</h3>
<ol>
  <li>Boil water.</li>
  <li>Add tea leaves and let them brew for 3 minutes.</li>
  <li>Add milk and sugar.</li>
  <li>Strain into a cup.</li>
</ol>

The browser numbers the items automatically. If you add or remove a step, the numbers update by themselves.

Changing the numbering

<ol> has a few useful attributes:

<ol type="A">
  <li>Option A</li>
  <li>Option B</li>
</ol>

<ol start="5">
  <li>This item is number 5</li>
  <li>This one is 6</li>
</ol>

<ol reversed>
  <li>Third place</li>
  <li>Second place</li>
  <li>Winner</li>
</ol>
  • type can be 1 (default), A, a, I or i.
  • start sets the first number.
  • reversed counts down.

Description lists

Use <dl> for pairs of terms and descriptions, like a glossary or a list of details:

<dl>
  <dt>HTML</dt>
  <dd>The language that gives a web page its structure.</dd>

  <dt>CSS</dt>
  <dd>The language that controls how the page looks.</dd>

  <dt>JavaScript</dt>
  <dd>The language that makes the page interactive.</dd>
</dl>
  • <dl> is the description list.
  • <dt> is the term.
  • <dd> is the description of that term.

Nested lists

A list item can contain another list. Put the inner list inside the <li>, before its closing tag:

<ul>
  <li>Frontend
    <ul>
      <li>HTML</li>
      <li>CSS</li>
      <li>JavaScript</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
  <li>Backend
    <ul>
      <li>Python</li>
      <li>SQL</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

Browsers indent nested lists and change the bullet style for each level.

Lists for navigation menus

Almost every website menu is a list of links inside a <nav> element:

<nav>
  <ul>
    <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
    <li><a href="/tutorials/">Tutorials</a></li>
    <li><a href="/blog/">Blog</a></li>
    <li><a href="/contact-us/">Contact</a></li>
  </ul>
</nav>

A menu *is* a list of choices, so this is the right meaning. Screen readers also announce "list, 4 items", which helps users know how big the menu is. With CSS you'll later remove the bullets and lay the links out in a row.

What can go inside a list

  • <ul> and <ol> may only contain <li> elements directly.
  • An <li> can contain almost anything: text, links, images, paragraphs, even other lists.
<!-- Wrong: text directly inside ul -->
<ul>
  Fruits
  <li>Apple</li>
</ul>

<!-- Right -->
<h4>Fruits</h4>
<ul>
  <li>Apple</li>
</ul>

Common mistakes

  • Typing bullet characters (• or -) at the start of paragraphs instead of using a real list.
  • **Closing the <li> before the nested list**, which places the inner list outside the item.
  • **Using <ol> for things with no order**, or <ul> for steps that must be followed in order.
  • **Putting headings or paragraphs directly in <ul>** without an <li>.

Exercise

  1. Make an unordered list of five programming languages.
  2. Make an ordered list with the steps to send an email.
  3. Create a nested list: three countries, each with two cities.
  4. Make a description list with three computer terms of your choice and their meanings.
  5. Build a small <nav> menu of four links using a list.

Summary

  • <ul> for unordered lists, <ol> for ordered lists, <li> for each item.
  • type, start and reversed change how ordered lists are numbered.
  • <dl>, <dt> and <dd> create description lists.
  • Nest a list inside an <li>; navigation menus are lists of links.

Next, you'll organise data in rows and columns with tables.
item.excerpt:encoded: Unordered, ordered and description lists, nested lists, numbering options and why navigation menus are built from lists.

item.title: HTML Tables
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Tables show data in rows and columns: timetables, price lists, results, comparisons. HTML tables are built from a handful of elements that fit together like a grid.

A first table

<table>
  <tr>
    <th>Name</th>
    <th>Language</th>
    <th>Score</th>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td>Asha</td>
    <td>Python</td>
    <td>92</td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td>Rohan</td>
    <td>JavaScript</td>
    <td>87</td>
  </tr>
</table>
  • <table> wraps the whole table.
  • <tr> (table row) creates a row.
  • <th> (table header) is a heading cell, shown bold and centred.
  • <td> (table data) is a normal cell.

Every row should have the same number of cells. By default, tables have no borders. You'll add them with CSS; for a quick test you can add border="1" to the <table> tag.

Captions

A <caption> gives the table a title. It must be the first thing inside <table>:

<table border="1">
  <caption>Class test results, March</caption>
  <tr>
    <th>Name</th>
    <th>Score</th>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td>Meera</td>
    <td>95</td>
  </tr>
</table>

Screen readers announce the caption before reading the table, so users know what they're about to hear.

Table sections: thead, tbody, tfoot

For larger tables, group the rows into sections:

<table border="1">
  <caption>Monthly expenses</caption>
  <thead>
    <tr>
      <th>Item</th>
      <th>Cost (₹)</th>
    </tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <td>Rent</td>
      <td>12,000</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Internet</td>
      <td>700</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Food</td>
      <td>6,500</td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
  <tfoot>
    <tr>
      <th>Total</th>
      <td>19,200</td>
    </tr>
  </tfoot>
</table>
  • <thead> holds the header rows.
  • <tbody> holds the main data.
  • <tfoot> holds summary rows such as totals.

These sections make the structure clear, make styling easier, and let browsers repeat the header on every printed page.

Row headers and the scope attribute

Headers can label rows as well as columns. scope tells assistive technology which way a header points:

<table border="1">
  <tr>
    <th scope="col">Day</th>
    <th scope="col">Morning</th>
    <th scope="col">Evening</th>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <th scope="row">Monday</th>
    <td>HTML</td>
    <td>Exercise</td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <th scope="row">Tuesday</th>
    <td>CSS</td>
    <td>Reading</td>
  </tr>
</table>

Merging cells: colspan and rowspan

colspan makes a cell stretch across several columns; rowspan makes it stretch down several rows.

<table border="1">
  <tr>
    <th>Time</th>
    <th>Monday</th>
    <th>Tuesday</th>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td>9:00</td>
    <td colspan="2">Team meeting (both days)</td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td>10:00</td>
    <td rowspan="2">Workshop</td>
    <td>Coding</td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td>11:00</td>
    <td>Review</td>
  </tr>
</table>

When a cell spans, the rows it covers have fewer <td> elements. In the last row above there are only two cells, because "Workshop" from the row before is still taking up the Monday column.

When not to use a table

Long ago, people built whole page layouts out of tables. Don't. Tables are for tabular data only: information that naturally has rows and columns. For page layout, use CSS Flexbox and Grid (you'll learn both in the CSS course). Layout tables confuse screen readers and are very hard to make work on phones.

Common mistakes

  • Different numbers of cells per row, which makes columns misalign.
  • **Using <td> for headings** with bold text instead of <th>.
  • **Putting the <caption> anywhere except first** inside <table>.
  • Forgetting to remove cells when using colspan or rowspan.
  • Using tables for layout.

Exercise

  1. Build a table of your weekly timetable: days as rows, three time slots as columns.
  2. Add a caption and <thead> / <tbody> sections.
  3. Use scope="row" on the day names.
  4. Merge two cells with colspan for an activity that lasts two slots.
  5. Add a <tfoot> row that counts the number of study sessions.

Summary

  • <table>, <tr>, <th> and <td> build the grid.
  • <caption>, <thead>, <tbody> and <tfoot> give it structure.
  • scope clarifies header direction; colspan and rowspan merge cells.
  • Use tables only for data, never for page layout.

Next, you'll meet the two general-purpose containers: div and span.
item.excerpt:encoded: Build tables with table, tr, th and td; add headers, captions and sections; merge cells with colspan and rowspan; and know when not to use a table.

item.title: HTML Div and Span
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
So far, every element you've used has a meaning: a heading, a paragraph, a link. Sometimes you just need a container to group things together so you can style or move them. That's what <div> and <span> are for. To use them well, you first need to understand block and inline elements.

Block elements

A block element starts on a new line and stretches across the full width available. Paragraphs, headings, lists and tables are all block elements.

<h3>A heading</h3>
<p>A paragraph.</p>
<p>Another paragraph.</p>

Each one sits on its own line, stacked from top to bottom.

Inline elements

An inline element stays inside the flow of text. It only takes as much width as its content and doesn't start a new line. Links, <strong>, <em>, <code> and <img> are inline.

<p>This sentence has a <a href="#">link</a>, some <strong>bold text</strong> and <code>code</code> in it.</p>

All of these stay on the same line as the surrounding text.

A simple rule: block elements can contain inline elements, but inline elements shouldn't contain block elements. For example, don't put a <p> inside a <strong>.

The div element

<div> (division) is a generic block container. It has no meaning and no default style; it simply groups other elements.

<div style="background: #eef6ff; padding: 16px; border-radius: 8px;">
  <h3>Tip of the day</h3>
  <p>Save your work often. Press Ctrl + S.</p>
</div>

Here the div groups a heading and a paragraph into one box so they can share a background colour. The style attribute adds a little CSS; you'll learn proper ways to do this in the CSS course.

Divs are used for:

  • Grouping elements to style them together (cards, boxes, columns).
  • Building page layouts with CSS Flexbox or Grid.
  • Giving JavaScript one element to show, hide or update.

The span element

<span> is a generic inline container. Use it to style or target a few words inside a line of text:

<p>Your order status: <span style="color: green; font-weight: bold;">Delivered</span></p>
<p>Total: <span id="total">₹0</span></p>

The first span colours one word. The second gives JavaScript a handle: a script could find #total and update the price without touching the rest of the paragraph.

Div vs span

Use meaningful elements first

Div and span have no meaning. Before reaching for them, ask: is there an element that describes this content?

<!-- Avoid: a div pretending to be a heading -->
<div style="font-size: 24px; font-weight: bold;">Our team</div>

<!-- Better -->
<h2>Our team</h2>

HTML also has meaningful containers like <header>, <nav>, <main>, <article>, <section> and <footer>. You'll learn them in the Semantic Elements lesson. Use those when they fit; use a div only when nothing else does.

Similarly, never build a clickable "button" from a div or span. Use a real <button>, which works with the keyboard and screen readers automatically.

A small card layout

<div style="border: 1px solid #ccc; border-radius: 8px; padding: 16px; max-width: 280px;">
  <img src="https://picsum.photos/id/20/280/160" alt="A laptop on a desk" width="280" height="160">
  <h3>Learn HTML</h3>
  <p>20 lessons · <span style="color: #2563eb;">Beginner</span></p>
  <a href="#">Start learning</a>
</div>

One div wraps the whole card; one span highlights a single word inside the text.

Common mistakes

  • "Divitis": wrapping everything in many layers of divs. Keep the structure as simple as possible.
  • Divs instead of headings, lists or buttons. Use the element with the right meaning.
  • Putting a div inside a span or a paragraph. A block can't go inside inline content.

Exercise

  1. Create two "tip boxes" with divs, each with a different background colour, a heading and a paragraph.
  2. In a sentence, use spans to colour the words "red", "green" and "blue" in their own colours.
  3. Build a profile card for yourself like the example above.

Summary

  • Block elements start on a new line and fill the width; inline elements stay in the text.
  • <div> is a generic block container; <span> is a generic inline container.
  • Neither has any meaning, so use meaningful elements first.
  • Divs and spans are mainly used as hooks for CSS and JavaScript.

Next, you'll learn how to name elements with classes and ids.
item.excerpt:encoded: Block and inline elements explained, and how the generic div and span containers group content for styling and scripting.

item.title: HTML Classes and IDs
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
As pages grow, you need a way to say "these five boxes should look the same" or "this one element is the shopping cart". The class and id attributes give elements names that CSS and JavaScript can use.

The class attribute

A class is a label you can give to any number of elements:

<style>
  .note {
    background: #fff7d6;
    border-left: 4px solid #f2b705;
    padding: 8px 12px;
  }
</style>

<p class="note">Remember to save your file before refreshing the browser.</p>
<p>A normal paragraph.</p>
<p class="note">File names are case-sensitive on most servers.</p>

The CSS rule .note (with a dot) styles every element that has class="note". Change the rule once, and every note on the site changes.

Several classes on one element

Separate class names with spaces:

<style>
  .btn { padding: 8px 16px; border-radius: 6px; border: none; }
  .btn-primary { background: #2563eb; color: white; }
  .btn-large { font-size: 20px; }
</style>

<button class="btn btn-primary">Save</button>
<button class="btn btn-primary btn-large">Sign up</button>
<button class="btn">Cancel</button>

This is how most real-world CSS works: small, reusable classes combined on each element.

The id attribute

An id is a unique name: only one element on a page may have a given id.

<style>
  #site-title { color: #2563eb; }
</style>

<h1 id="site-title">VitalStack</h1>

In CSS, an id is selected with #. Ids have three main uses:

  • Links to a section: <a href="#pricing"> jumps to id="pricing".
  • JavaScript: document.getElementById("cart") finds exactly one element.
  • Forms: a <label for="email"> is connected to the input with id="email".

Class vs id

A good habit: use classes for styling and keep ids for links, forms and JavaScript. Id rules in CSS are very "strong" and hard to override later, which you'll understand in the CSS Selectors lesson.

Classes and ids in JavaScript

<p id="greeting">Hello!</p>
<button class="change">Change greeting</button>

<script>
  document.querySelector(".change").addEventListener("click", function () {
    document.getElementById("greeting").textContent = "Welcome to VitalStack!";
  });
</script>

Click the button and the paragraph text changes. The script found the button by its class and the paragraph by its id. You'll learn this properly in the JavaScript course.

Naming rules and good habits

  • Names are case-sensitive: Note and note are different.
  • Don't use spaces inside one name (a space means "two classes"). Use hyphens: main-menu, card-title.
  • Don't start a name with a number.
  • Name things by what they are, not how they look: .warning is better than .red-text, because you might change the colour to orange next year.
  • Keep names short, lowercase and consistent across the site.

Common mistakes

  • The same id twice on a page. Links and JavaScript will only find the first one.
  • **Using . or # in the HTML attribute.** Write class="note", not class=".note". The dot belongs in CSS only.
  • **Writing class="btn" class="large".** Only the first one counts. Use class="btn large".
  • Naming by appearance, which makes names lie after a redesign.

Exercise

  1. Create a .card class with a border and padding, and use it on three divs.
  2. Add a second class .featured with a different background, and apply it to one of the cards as well.
  3. Give your page a heading with id="top" and add a "Back to top" link at the bottom.
  4. Change the button example so the button's text also changes after it's clicked.

Summary

  • class labels any number of elements; select them in CSS with .name.
  • id names one unique element; select it with #name.
  • An element can have many classes, separated by spaces.
  • Use classes for styling, ids for links, labels and JavaScript.

Next, you'll start collecting information from users with HTML forms.
item.excerpt:encoded: Name elements with the class and id attributes, use them from CSS and JavaScript, and learn the naming rules that keep a project tidy.

item.title: HTML Forms
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Every sign-up page, search box, contact page and checkout is a form. Forms let visitors send information to a website. In this lesson you'll build a complete basic form and understand what happens when it's submitted.

A first form

<form action="/subscribe" method="post">
  <label for="name">Your name</label>
  <input type="text" id="name" name="name">

  <label for="email">Email</label>
  <input type="email" id="email" name="email">

  <button type="submit">Subscribe</button>
</form>

That's a working form with two fields and a button. Let's look at each part.

The form element

<form> wraps all the fields that are sent together. Its two most important attributes are:

  • action: the URL that receives the data. If you leave it out, the form submits to the current page.
  • method: how the data is sent, get or post.

GET or POST?

A search form is a perfect GET form:

<form action="https://www.google.com/search" method="get">
  <label for="q">Search Google</label>
  <input type="search" id="q" name="q">
  <button type="submit">Search</button>
</form>

Type a word and submit: you'll see ?q=yourword added to the address.

Labels

A <label> describes a field. Connect it to the field by making the label's for match the input's id:

<label for="city">City</label>
<input type="text" id="city" name="city">

Why this matters:

  • Clicking the label puts the cursor in the field, a bigger target on phones.
  • Screen readers read the label when the field gets focus. Without it, the user just hears "edit text" and has to guess.

You can also wrap the input inside the label, which connects them without for/id:

<label>City <input type="text" name="city"></label>

The name attribute

name is the key the data is sent with. A field without a name is not sent at all.

If someone types "Asha" into <input name="name"> and "asha@example.com" into <input name="email">, the server receives:

name=Asha&email=asha%40example.com

The id is for the page (labels, CSS, JavaScript); the name is for the server. They often have the same value, which is fine.

Placeholder and value

<label for="phone">Phone</label>
<input type="tel" id="phone" name="phone" placeholder="98765 43210">

<label for="country">Country</label>
<input type="text" id="country" name="country" value="India">
  • placeholder shows a light example inside an empty field. It disappears when the user types, so it should never replace the label.
  • value sets the starting content of the field. The user can change it.

Textarea for longer text

<label for="message">Message</label>
<textarea id="message" name="message" rows="5" cols="40"></textarea>

<textarea> is a multi-line text box. It has a closing tag; any text between the tags becomes its starting value.

Buttons

<button type="submit">Send</button>
<button type="reset">Clear form</button>
<button type="button">Does nothing by itself</button>
  • submit sends the form (this is the default for a button inside a form).
  • reset clears all fields back to their starting values; rarely useful, and easy to click by mistake.
  • button does nothing unless JavaScript gives it a job.

Grouping with fieldset and legend

<form>
  <fieldset>
    <legend>Delivery address</legend>
    <label for="street">Street</label>
    <input type="text" id="street" name="street">
    <label for="pin">PIN code</label>
    <input type="text" id="pin" name="pin">
  </fieldset>
  <button type="submit">Continue</button>
</form>

<fieldset> draws a box around related fields, and <legend> gives the group a title that screen readers announce.

Common mistakes

  • No labels, only placeholders. The hint vanishes as soon as the user types.
  • **Missing name** on a field, so its value is never sent.
  • **for and id that don't match** exactly (they're case-sensitive).
  • Sending passwords with GET, which puts them in the address bar and browser history.

Exercise

Build a "Contact us" form with:

  1. Name and email fields, each with a label.
  2. A subject field with a placeholder example.
  3. A message <textarea>.
  4. A submit button that says "Send message".
  5. Group name and email in a <fieldset> with the legend "Your details".

Submit it with method="get" and look at the URL to see exactly what would be sent.

Summary

  • <form> wraps fields; action says where data goes, method says how.
  • Use GET for searches, POST for anything private or that changes data.
  • Every field needs a <label> and a name.
  • <textarea> handles long text; <button type="submit"> sends the form.

Next, you'll learn all the input types: checkboxes, radio buttons, dropdowns, dates and built-in validation.
item.excerpt:encoded: How forms collect information: the form element, action and method, labels, text inputs, the name attribute and submit buttons.

item.title: HTML Form Inputs
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
The <input> element changes completely depending on its type. One attribute turns a plain text box into a date picker, a slider or a checkbox. Choosing the right type gives users the right keyboard on their phone and gives you free validation.

Text-like inputs

<form>
  <label for="u">Username</label>
  <input type="text" id="u" name="username"><br><br>

  <label for="e">Email</label>
  <input type="email" id="e" name="email"><br><br>

  <label for="p">Password</label>
  <input type="password" id="p" name="password"><br><br>

  <label for="t">Phone</label>
  <input type="tel" id="t" name="phone"><br><br>

  <label for="w">Website</label>
  <input type="url" id="w" name="website"><br><br>

  <button>Send</button>
</form>
  • email checks for an @ and shows an email keyboard on phones.
  • password hides the characters.
  • tel shows a number pad on phones (it doesn't check the format, because phone formats differ by country).
  • url checks for a full web address.

Numbers, ranges and dates

<label for="qty">Quantity (1–10)</label>
<input type="number" id="qty" name="qty" min="1" max="10" value="1"><br><br>

<label for="vol">Volume</label>
<input type="range" id="vol" name="volume" min="0" max="100" step="5"><br><br>

<label for="dob">Date of birth</label>
<input type="date" id="dob" name="dob"><br><br>

<label for="time">Meeting time</label>
<input type="time" id="time" name="time"><br><br>

<label for="fav">Favourite colour</label>
<input type="color" id="fav" name="colour" value="#2563eb">

min, max and step limit what can be chosen. Date and time inputs show the device's own calendar or clock picker.

Checkboxes

Checkboxes let users pick any number of options:

<p>Which languages do you know?</p>
<label><input type="checkbox" name="langs" value="html"> HTML</label><br>
<label><input type="checkbox" name="langs" value="css" checked> CSS</label><br>
<label><input type="checkbox" name="langs" value="js"> JavaScript</label>
  • value is what gets sent when the box is ticked (if you leave it out, the browser sends "on").
  • checked ticks the box from the start.
  • Unticked boxes send nothing.

Radio buttons

Radio buttons let users pick exactly one option from a group. Buttons with the **same name** form one group:

<p>Choose a plan:</p>
<label><input type="radio" name="plan" value="free" checked> Free</label><br>
<label><input type="radio" name="plan" value="pro"> Pro</label><br>
<label><input type="radio" name="plan" value="team"> Team</label>

Clicking one automatically un-selects the others. If each radio had a different name, they'd all be selectable at once, the most common radio-button bug.

Dropdowns with select

<label for="course">Course</label>
<select id="course" name="course">
  <option value="">Choose a course…</option>
  <option value="html">HTML</option>
  <option value="css">CSS</option>
  <option value="js" selected>JavaScript</option>
</select>

Use <optgroup label="..."> to group long lists, and add multiple to let users pick several options (though checkboxes are usually easier for that).

File uploads and hidden fields

<label for="cv">Upload your CV (PDF)</label>
<input type="file" id="cv" name="cv" accept=".pdf">

<input type="hidden" name="source" value="newsletter">

A form with a file input must use method="post" and enctype="multipart/form-data". Hidden inputs send a value the user doesn't see, such as which page the form came from.

Built-in validation

The browser can check fields before the form is sent, with no JavaScript:

<form>
  <label for="n">Name (required)</label>
  <input type="text" id="n" name="name" required minlength="2"><br><br>

  <label for="age">Age (13–120)</label>
  <input type="number" id="age" name="age" min="13" max="120"><br><br>

  <label for="pin">PIN code (6 digits)</label>
  <input type="text" id="pin" name="pin" pattern="[0-9]{6}" title="Six digits, e.g. 400001"><br><br>

  <button>Submit</button>
</form>

Try submitting it empty or with wrong values: the browser stops and shows a message.

  • required: the field can't be empty.
  • minlength / maxlength: text length limits.
  • min / max: number and date limits.
  • pattern: a regular expression the value must match; describe the format in title or near the field.

Important: browser validation helps users, but anyone can bypass it. A server must always check the data again.

Other useful attributes

  • disabled: the field can't be used and isn't sent.
  • readonly: the field can't be changed but is sent.
  • autocomplete="email" (or name, tel, street-address…): lets the browser fill in saved details.
  • autofocus: puts the cursor in this field when the page loads (use once, at most).

Common mistakes

  • Radio buttons with different names, so more than one can be selected.
  • **Using type="text" for everything**, missing the right phone keyboards and free checks.
  • Trusting browser validation alone. Always validate on the server too.
  • **Checkboxes without value**, so the server receives "on" with no idea which option it was.

Exercise

Build a course registration form with:

  1. Name (required), email (type email, required) and age (13–100).
  2. A dropdown of three courses.
  3. Radio buttons for "Morning" or "Evening" batch.
  4. Checkboxes for "I have a laptop" and "Send me updates".
  5. A start date picker.

Try to submit it with empty and wrong values and read the browser's messages.

Summary

  • The type attribute turns <input> into the right control for each kind of data.
  • Checkboxes allow many choices; radio buttons with the same name allow one.
  • <select> creates a dropdown from <option> elements.
  • required, min, max, minlength and pattern give free validation, but the server must check again.

Next, you'll learn semantic elements that describe the structure of a whole page.
item.excerpt:encoded: Every common input type, from email, number and date to checkboxes, radio buttons and dropdowns, plus built-in validation with required, min, max and pattern.

item.title: HTML Semantic Elements
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
"Semantic" means "related to meaning". A semantic element tells the browser what its content is, not just how to show it. <h1> and <p> are semantic; <div> isn't. HTML has a set of semantic elements for the big parts of a page: the header, the menu, the main content, the sidebar and the footer.

The page layout elements

Most websites follow the same pattern:

<body>
  <header>
    <h1>My Coding Blog</h1>
    <nav>
      <ul>
        <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
        <li><a href="/blog/">Blog</a></li>
        <li><a href="/about/">About</a></li>
      </ul>
    </nav>
  </header>

  <main>
    <article>
      <h2>How I learned HTML in 30 days</h2>
      <p>It started with one simple page…</p>
    </article>
  </main>

  <aside>
    <h3>Popular posts</h3>
    <ul>
      <li><a href="#">10 CSS tips</a></li>
    </ul>
  </aside>

  <footer>
    <p><small>© My Coding Blog</small></p>
  </footer>
</body>

Without any CSS this looks the same as a pile of divs, but the code now describes the page.

What each element means

header

Introductory content: a site logo and title, or the heading area of an article. A page can have several headers: one for the site and one inside each article.

nav

A block of major navigation links: the main menu, a table of contents, pagination. Not every group of links needs <nav>; footer links to legal pages, for example, usually don't.

main

The main content of the page, the part that's unique to it. There should be only one visible <main> per page, and it shouldn't include things repeated on every page like the site header, menu or footer.

article

A self-contained piece of content that would make sense on its own, even if copied to another site: a blog post, a news story, a product card, a forum post, a comment.

section

A thematic group of content, usually with its own heading: "Features", "Pricing", "FAQ". If you can't think of a heading for it, you probably want a <div> instead.

aside

Content that's related but not essential: a sidebar, a "did you know?" box, related links, ads.

footer

The closing part of a page or an article: copyright, contact details, related links, author info.

Article or section?

A simple test: would it make sense on its own? Then it's an <article>. Is it one part of something bigger? Then it's a <section>. They can also be nested both ways:

<article>
  <h2>Getting Started with Python</h2>
  <section>
    <h3>Installing Python</h3>
    <p>Download it from python.org…</p>
  </section>
  <section>
    <h3>Your first program</h3>
    <p>Open your editor and type print("Hello")…</p>
  </section>
</article>

Other useful semantic elements

<p>Published on <time datetime="2026-03-14">14 March</time></p>

<details>
  <summary>What is a semantic element?</summary>
  <p>An element whose name describes the meaning of its content.</p>
</details>

<address>
  Written by Asha. Contact: <a href="mailto:asha@example.com">asha@example.com</a>
</address>
  • <time> marks a date or time; datetime gives it in a format computers understand.
  • <details> and <summary> create a collapsible box with no JavaScript. Great for FAQs.
  • <address> holds contact information for the author or owner.
  • <figure> and <figcaption>, from the images lesson, are semantic too.

Why semantic HTML matters

  • Accessibility. Screen readers announce landmarks like "navigation" and "main", and let users jump straight to them. A "skip to content" experience comes almost for free.
  • Search engines understand which part is the real content and which part is the menu or footer.
  • Readable code. </article> tells you far more than the seventh </div> in a row.
  • Reader modes in browsers use these elements to show a clean version of your page.

Common mistakes

  • **More than one <main>** on a page.
  • **Wrapping everything in <section>**, even blocks with no heading. Use <div> for pure styling groups.
  • **Using <aside> for main content**, just because it's displayed in a side column.
  • Forgetting headings inside sections and articles.

Exercise

Take any page you've built in this course (or start a new one) and:

  1. Wrap the title and menu in <header> and <nav>.
  2. Put the main content in <main> with one <article> and two <section>s inside it.
  3. Add an <aside> with three related links.
  4. Add a <footer> with a copyright line.
  5. Add a FAQ with two <details> boxes.

Summary

  • Semantic elements describe meaning: <header>, <nav>, <main>, <article>, <section>, <aside>, <footer>.
  • One <main> per page; <article> stands alone; <section> is a themed part with a heading.
  • <time>, <details>/<summary> and <address> add meaning to smaller pieces.
  • Semantic HTML helps accessibility, search engines and your own code.

Next, you'll add audio and video to your pages.
item.excerpt:encoded: Describe the parts of a page with header, nav, main, article, section, aside and footer, and see why meaningful HTML helps readers and search engines.

item.title: HTML Media (Audio and Video)
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Before HTML5, playing a video on a web page needed a plugin like Flash. Today the browser does it on its own with two elements: <video> and <audio>. In this lesson you'll use both, add captions, and embed videos from YouTube.

The video element

<video src="https://interactive-examples.mdn.mozilla.net/media/cc0-videos/flower.mp4"
       width="400" height="225" controls>
  Your browser does not support the video element.
</video>
  • src is the video file.
  • controls shows the play button, timeline and volume. Without it, the user has no way to start the video.
  • width and height reserve space, just like with images.
  • The text inside the tags only appears in very old browsers that can't play video.

Useful video attributes

<video src="https://interactive-examples.mdn.mozilla.net/media/cc0-videos/flower.mp4"
       width="400" height="225"
       controls muted loop playsinline
       poster="https://picsum.photos/id/106/400/225"
       preload="metadata">
</video>
  • poster: an image shown before the video starts.
  • muted: starts with sound off.
  • loop: starts again at the end.
  • autoplay: starts playing by itself. Browsers only allow this if the video is also muted, because surprise sound is annoying.
  • playsinline: on iPhones, plays inside the page instead of going full-screen.
  • preload: none, metadata (just the length and size) or auto. Use none or metadata to save your readers' mobile data.

Several formats with source

Not every browser supports every format. You can list several files and the browser picks the first one it can play:

<video width="400" height="225" controls>
  <source src="movie.webm" type="video/webm">
  <source src="movie.mp4" type="video/mp4">
  Sorry, your browser can't play this video.
</video>

Today MP4 (H.264) plays in every modern browser, so a single MP4 file is usually enough. WebM files are often smaller, so listing WebM first and MP4 as a fallback is a common pattern.

The audio element

<audio controls src="https://interactive-examples.mdn.mozilla.net/media/cc0-audio/t-rex-roar.mp3">
  Your browser does not support the audio element.
</audio>

<audio> works just like <video>, with controls, loop, muted, preload and <source> elements. MP3 plays everywhere.

Captions and subtitles with track

Captions help deaf and hard-of-hearing viewers, people watching without sound (most mobile viewers), and people who speak another language.

<video width="400" height="225" controls>
  <source src="lesson.mp4" type="video/mp4">
  <track src="lesson-en.vtt" kind="captions" srclang="en" label="English" default>
  <track src="lesson-hi.vtt" kind="subtitles" srclang="hi" label="Hindi">
</video>

Caption files use the simple WebVTT format:

WEBVTT

00:00:00.000 --> 00:00:04.000
Welcome to the HTML video lesson.

00:00:04.000 --> 00:00:08.000
Today we'll add captions to a video.

Embedding YouTube videos with iframe

Video files are large, and streaming them from your own hosting can be slow and expensive. For long videos, upload them to YouTube and embed them with an <iframe> (an element that shows another web page inside yours):

<iframe width="400" height="225"
        src="https://www.youtube-nocookie.com/embed/VIDEO_ID"
        title="Lesson video: HTML basics"
        loading="lazy"
        allow="accelerometer; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture"
        allowfullscreen></iframe>

Replace VIDEO_ID with the code from the video's address (the part after watch?v=). YouTube's Share → Embed button gives you this code ready-made.

  • title describes the frame for screen readers. Always add it.
  • loading="lazy" delays loading until the reader scrolls near it, which saves a lot of data.
  • youtube-nocookie.com is YouTube's privacy-friendlier version that doesn't set tracking cookies until the user plays the video.

Good practice with media

  • Never autoplay with sound.
  • Provide captions for videos with speech and a transcript for audio such as podcasts. Transcripts also help search engines understand the content.
  • Keep files small: compress videos and use a sensible resolution (720p is plenty for most lesson clips).
  • Don't put essential information *only* in a video. Some readers can't or won't play it.

Common mistakes

  • **Forgetting controls**, which leaves an un-playable box.
  • **Autoplay without muted**: the browser blocks it.
  • Huge video files on cheap hosting, which make pages slow. Use YouTube or a video host.
  • **An iframe without a title.**

Exercise

  1. Add the flower video with controls, a poster image and preload="metadata".
  2. Make a muted, looping version without controls, like a background clip.
  3. Add the audio example.
  4. Embed any YouTube video using its Share → Embed code, and add a title and loading="lazy".

Summary

  • <video> and <audio> play media without plugins; add controls.
  • Use <source> for several formats and <track> for captions.
  • Autoplay only works muted, and should be rare.
  • Embed long videos from YouTube with an <iframe> that has a title.

Next, you'll learn accessibility basics: how to make sure everyone can use your pages.
item.excerpt:encoded: Play sound and video with the audio and video elements, offer several file formats, add captions, and embed YouTube videos with iframe.

item.title: HTML Accessibility Basics

item.content:encoded:
Accessibility (often shortened to a11y: "a", eleven letters, "y") means building pages that everyone can use, including people who are blind, have low vision, are deaf, can't use a mouse, or have trouble reading. The good news: if you've followed this course, you're already doing most of it, because accessible HTML is mostly *correct* HTML.

Who benefits

  • Screen reader users (blind or low vision) hear the page read aloud and navigate by headings, links and landmarks.
  • Keyboard users (people with motor disabilities, power users) move through the page with Tab, Enter and the arrow keys.
  • People who zoom the page to 200% or more.
  • Deaf and hard-of-hearing users rely on captions and transcripts.
  • Everyone else, sometimes: a broken arm, bright sunlight on a phone screen, a slow connection, a noisy train.

Accessible sites also tend to rank better in search, because search engines "read" pages in a similar way to screen readers.

1. Use the right element

The single biggest rule. Native elements come with built-in keyboard support and meaning:

<!-- Bad: looks like a button, but keyboard users can't reach or press it -->
<div class="btn" onclick="save()">Save</div>

<!-- Good: focusable, works with Enter and Space, announced as "button" -->
<button type="button" onclick="save()">Save</button>

Use <button> for actions, <a href> for going somewhere, headings for titles, lists for lists.

2. Text alternatives

<img src="team.jpg" alt="Our five team members at the 2025 hackathon">
<img src="divider.png" alt="">

Every image needs alt: a description for meaningful images, empty for decoration. Videos need captions; audio needs a transcript.

3. Label every form field

<label for="email">Email address</label>
<input type="email" id="email" name="email" autocomplete="email">

A placeholder is not a label. Error messages should be in text near the field and say how to fix the problem ("Enter an email like name@example.com"), not just turn the field red.

4. A clear heading structure

One <h1>, then <h2> and <h3> in order. Many screen reader users jump from heading to heading to find what they need, just as sighted users skim.

5. Landmarks

<header>…</header>
<nav aria-label="Main">…</nav>
<main>…</main>
<footer>…</footer>

Semantic layout elements become landmarks that screen readers list and jump to. If you have two <nav>s, give each an aria-label so users can tell them apart.

6. Keyboard access and focus

Try this now: put your mouse away and press Tab to move through any website. You should:

  • Reach every link, button and field, in a logical order.
  • Always see where you are (the focus outline).
  • Be able to activate everything with Enter or Space.

Never remove the focus outline with CSS (outline: none) unless you replace it with another clear style.

A skip link lets keyboard users jump past the menu:

<a href="#main" class="skip-link">Skip to content</a>
<header>…long menu…</header>
<main id="main">…</main>

7. Colour and contrast

  • Text needs enough contrast with its background: at least 4.5:1 for normal text. Light grey on white often fails. Browser developer tools can check contrast for you.
  • Never use colour alone to carry meaning. "Fields in red are required" fails for colour-blind users; add a word or symbol: "Email (required)".

8. Language and page title

<html lang="en">
<head>
  <title>Contact us · VitalStack</title>
</head>

lang makes screen readers use the right pronunciation. A unique, descriptive <title> is the first thing a screen reader announces on a new page.

9. ARIA: only when HTML isn't enough

ARIA attributes add extra information for assistive technology:

<button aria-label="Close menu">✕</button>
<button aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="menu">Menu</button>
<p role="alert">Your message has been sent.</p>
  • aria-label gives a name to an element with no visible text, like an icon button.
  • aria-expanded tells users whether a menu is open.
  • role="alert" makes a screen reader announce a message immediately.

The first rule of ARIA: don't use ARIA if a native element does the job. A <button> is better than <div role="button">. Wrong ARIA is worse than none.

Quick checklist

  • ☐ Every image has suitable alt text.
  • ☐ Every form field has a label.
  • ☐ Headings are in order; one <h1>.
  • ☐ Everything works with the keyboard, and focus is visible.
  • ☐ Text contrast is strong enough; colour is never the only signal.
  • ☐ lang and a unique <title> are set.
  • ☐ Videos have captions.

Common mistakes

  • Clickable divs and spans instead of buttons and links.
  • Removing focus outlines for looks.
  • "Click here" links and icon buttons with no name.
  • Adding ARIA everywhere instead of using the right HTML.

Exercise

  1. Take your form from the Form Inputs lesson and check every field has a working label (click each label: the field should get focus).
  2. Use only the Tab key to fill in and submit the form.
  3. Add a "Skip to content" link to your semantic page from lesson 17.
  4. Find an icon-only button (like ✕) and give it an aria-label.

Summary

  • Accessible HTML is mostly correct, semantic HTML.
  • Alt text, labels, headings, landmarks and visible focus cover most needs.
  • Check contrast and never use colour alone.
  • Use ARIA only when native HTML can't express what you need.

item.title: HTML Project: Build a Personal Profile Page
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Time to use everything you've learned. In this project you'll build a complete personal profile page: a header with a menu, an about section, a skills list, a projects table, a contact form and a footer. It's pure HTML for now; in the CSS course you'll make it beautiful.

What you'll build

The finished page has:

  1. A header with your name and a navigation menu that jumps to each section.
  2. An "About me" section with a photo and a short introduction.
  3. A "Skills" section with a nested list.
  4. A "Projects" table.
  5. A "Contact" form.
  6. A FAQ with collapsible answers.
  7. A footer.

Work step by step. After each step, check the result with Try it Yourself or in your own editor.

Step 1: The skeleton

Start with the basic structure from lesson 3 and the semantic layout from lesson 17:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
  <title>Asha Verma · Web Developer</title>
</head>
<body>
  <a href="#main">Skip to content</a>

  <header>
    <h1>Asha Verma</h1>
    <p>Beginner web developer from Pune</p>
    <nav aria-label="Main">
      <ul>
        <li><a href="#about">About</a></li>
        <li><a href="#skills">Skills</a></li>
        <li><a href="#projects">Projects</a></li>
        <li><a href="#contact">Contact</a></li>
      </ul>
    </nav>
  </header>

  <main id="main">
    <!-- sections go here -->
  </main>

  <footer>
    <p><small>© Asha Verma. Built with plain HTML.</small></p>
  </footer>
</body>
</html>

Replace the name, city and title with your own (or invent a character). Notice the menu links point to ids you'll create next.

Step 2: About me

Inside <main>, add the first section:

<section id="about">
  <h2>About me</h2>
  <figure>
    <img src="https://picsum.photos/id/64/240/240" alt="Asha smiling, sitting at a desk with a laptop" width="240" height="240">
    <figcaption>Learning to code, one lesson a day.</figcaption>
  </figure>
  <p>Hi! I'm Asha. I started learning web development in January and I'm <strong>building one small project every week</strong>.</p>
  <p>Before coding, I worked in <em>customer support</em>, which taught me to explain things clearly. Now I want to build websites that are <mark>simple and easy to use</mark>.</p>
</section>

You used: a heading, a figure with an image and caption, paragraphs, and text formatting.

Step 3: Skills

<section id="skills">
  <h2>Skills</h2>
  <ul>
    <li>Frontend
      <ul>
        <li>HTML: semantic pages, forms, tables</li>
        <li>CSS: learning now</li>
      </ul>
    </li>
    <li>Tools
      <ul>
        <li>VS Code</li>
        <li>Browser developer tools</li>
      </ul>
    </li>
  </ul>

  <h3>Learning plan</h3>
  <ol>
    <li>Finish the HTML course</li>
    <li>Learn CSS layout with Flexbox and Grid</li>
    <li>Start JavaScript</li>
  </ol>
</section>

An unordered list for skills (no order), an ordered list for the plan (order matters).

Step 4: Projects table

<section id="projects">
  <h2>Projects</h2>
  <table border="1">
    <caption>Things I've built so far</caption>
    <thead>
      <tr>
        <th scope="col">Project</th>
        <th scope="col">What I learned</th>
        <th scope="col">Link</th>
      </tr>
    </thead>
    <tbody>
      <tr>
        <th scope="row">Recipe page</th>
        <td>Headings, lists and images</td>
        <td><a href="#">View</a></td>
      </tr>
      <tr>
        <th scope="row">Timetable</th>
        <td>Tables with colspan</td>
        <td><a href="#">View</a></td>
      </tr>
      <tr>
        <th scope="row">This profile</th>
        <td>Putting it all together</td>
        <td><a href="#main">You're here</a></td>
      </tr>
    </tbody>
  </table>
</section>

Step 5: Contact form

<section id="contact">
  <h2>Contact me</h2>
  <form action="https://example.com/contact" method="post">
    <fieldset>
      <legend>Your details</legend>
      <p>
        <label for="name">Name</label><br>
        <input type="text" id="name" name="name" autocomplete="name" required>
      </p>
      <p>
        <label for="email">Email</label><br>
        <input type="email" id="email" name="email" autocomplete="email" required>
      </p>
    </fieldset>

    <p>Reason for contacting:</p>
    <p>
      <label><input type="radio" name="reason" value="project" checked> A project</label><br>
      <label><input type="radio" name="reason" value="hello"> Just saying hello</label>
    </p>

    <p>
      <label for="message">Message</label><br>
      <textarea id="message" name="message" rows="5" cols="40" required minlength="10"></textarea>
    </p>

    <button type="submit">Send message</button>
  </form>
</section>

Labels on every field, the right input types, validation, and grouped radio buttons.

Step 6: FAQ

<section id="faq">
  <h2>FAQ</h2>
  <details>
    <summary>Are you available for freelance work?</summary>
    <p>Small HTML and CSS projects, yes. Use the contact form.</p>
  </details>
  <details>
    <summary>How long have you been coding?</summary>
    <p>Since <time datetime="2026-01">January 2026</time>.</p>
  </details>
</section>

Step 7: Check your work

Go through this checklist:

  • ☐ Every menu link jumps to the right section.
  • ☐ Only one <h1>; headings go h2 → h3 without skipping.
  • ☐ Every image has alt text, width and height.
  • ☐ Every form field has a label; submitting empty fields shows browser messages.
  • ☐ You can reach every link and field using only the Tab key.
  • ☐ No ids are repeated.

For a final check, paste your page into the free W3C Markup Validator (validator.w3.org, "Validate by Direct Input"). It lists any mistakes in your HTML; fix them until it shows no errors.

Ideas to extend it

  • Add a "Currently learning" section with a short <blockquote> from a favourite programmer.
  • Add a short YouTube video introducing yourself, with loading="lazy" and a title.
  • Make a second page, projects.html, and link between the two pages.

What you've learned in this course

Over 20 lessons you've gone from "what is HTML?" to a complete, accessible, semantic page. You can now structure text, links, images, lists, tables, forms and media, and you know how to make pages that work for everyone.

Summary

  • A complete page combines structure, content and forms inside semantic landmarks.
  • Check menus, headings, alt text, labels and keyboard access before calling it done.
  • The W3C validator is a free way to find mistakes.

Next comes the CSS course, where you'll take this exact page and give it colours, fonts, spacing and a modern layout.
